items.prompt: During some work, GC.CollectionCount(2) went up by 1. What is the least you know about GC.CollectionCount(0) over the same work?
items.answer: It rose by at least 1, as a gen2 pass also counts as gen0
distractors: Nothing; the counters for each generation are independent
It stayed the same, since a gen2 pass skips gen0 entirely
It fell by 1, because survivors moved out of gen0
items.explanation: The counters are cumulative upward: a gen2 collection also collects gen1 and gen0, so CollectionCount(0) includes gen1 and gen2 passes.

items.prompt: ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Rent(1000) returns an array whose Length is 1024. How many bytes should your code treat as its payload?
items.answer: The 1000 you asked for, tracked in your own variable
distractors: buffer.Length, because Rent sizes the array to fit the request
All 1024; the pool zero-fills the extra 24 for you
Whatever Return reports once clearArray has run
items.explanation: Rent(n) gives at least n. The guide comments the copy length as Math.Min(chunkSize, remaining) and says NEVER buffer.Length: the tail may hold stale data from earlier renters.

items.prompt: A struct value is added to a List<T> of that struct type. Where does the stored value live?
items.answer: Inside the list's backing array, which is on the heap
distractors: On the stack frame of the method that called Add
In its own boxed heap object, one per element
In a runtime pool of structs, kept per thread
items.explanation: A List<T> of a value type stores the values inline in its T[] array, which is a heap object. No boxing is involved; boxing happens when a struct is cast to object or an interface.

items.prompt: Several threads call cache.GetOrAdd(key, k => OpenConnection(k)) at once for the same new key on a ConcurrentDictionary. What can happen?
items.answer: The factory may run on several threads; the losers' connections leak
distractors: It runs exactly once, since GetOrAdd holds a lock around the factory
The other threads throw while the key is still being added
Each thread stores its own entry under the same key
items.explanation: ConcurrentDictionary deliberately does not hold a lock while your factory runs. Several factories can run; one value wins and the rest are discarded unclosed. Wrapping the value in Lazy<T> with ExecutionAndPublication makes the expensive part run once.

items.prompt: With today's Dictionary<TKey,TValue>, keys A, B and C are added, B is removed, then D is added. In what order does enumeration return the keys?
items.answer: A, D, C, because D reuses the slot that B left free
distractors: A, C, D, as enumeration always follows insertion order
D, A, C, since the newest key moves to the front
C, A, D, because removal compacts entries in reverse
items.explanation: The entries array keeps slots in place; Remove puts B's slot on a free list and the next Add reuses it, so D appears where B was. The guide warns against relying on order for this reason.

items.prompt: A method declares, in order: using var connection, then using var command, then using var reader. In what order are they disposed at the end of the scope?
distractors: connection, then command, then reader, in declaration order
Only connection; it disposes its own command and reader
Whatever order the finalizer thread happens to reach them
items.explanation: Each using is a try/finally nested inside the previous one, so the innermost (last declared) resource is released first. That order is required: disposing the connection first would run the command's cleanup against a closed connection.

items.prompt: A type implements IAsyncDisposable but not IDisposable. What happens when a caller writes a plain using statement on it?
items.answer: It does not compile, so callers must write await using
distractors: It compiles and calls DisposeAsync synchronously for you
It compiles, and disposal is skipped at runtime with no error
It compiles; it throws NotSupportedException at scope exit
items.explanation: A plain using requires IDisposable; with only IAsyncDisposable the compiler rejects it, which is why the guide recommends async-only types when release is real I/O.

items.prompt: An async Task method throws ArgumentNullException before its first await. The caller invokes it and stores the task without awaiting it. What happens at the call?
items.answer: No throw at the call, but the returned task is faulted
distractors: It throws synchronously at the call, before any task exists
The exception is swallowed and the task completes normally
It crashes the process at once as an unobserved exception
items.explanation: The compiler-generated state machine captures every exception from an async method body, including ones thrown before the first await, into the returned task. Callers who need a synchronous throw need a non-async wrapper that validates first.

items.prompt: Code runs await Task.WhenAll(t1, t2, t3), and both t1 and t3 fault. What does the await throw?
items.answer: The first inner exception, with the rest left on the task
distractors: An AggregateException that holds both of the two failures
Both of them, one after another, in completion order
Nothing until t2 also faults, and then all of them
items.explanation: await unwraps the faulted task and rethrows its first inner exception. The full set is in the WhenAll task's Exception.InnerExceptions; an AggregateException surfaces only through .Result or .Wait().

items.prompt: A catch block has a when filter, and the filter returns false for the exception being thrown. What happens to that exception?
items.answer: It keeps propagating, same object and same stack trace
distractors: It is caught and rethrown, which resets its stack trace
It is swallowed, because a filter acts as the catch body
It is wrapped in an AggregateException and then rethrown
items.explanation: Filters run before the stack unwinds; a false result means the catch never runs, so the exception continues untouched, which catch-then-throw; cannot fully claim.

items.prompt: A method creates new JsonSerializerOptions() every time it serializes an object. Why is that expensive?
items.answer: Type metadata is cached per options instance, so it is rebuilt
distractors: Each instance opens a new pooled UTF-8 buffer that is never freed
The serializer must recompile its source generator on each call
Options objects are finalizable, so each one survives a GC
items.explanation: The serializer caches a JsonTypeInfo per type per options instance. A fresh instance re-derives everything by reflection; one static shared instance avoids it.

items.prompt: Version 2 of a DTO adds a new property and marks it required. What happens to version 1 documents that lack it?
items.answer: They now fail to deserialize, since the member is missing
distractors: They deserialize, and the property gets its default value
They deserialize; the property lands in extension data
They deserialize, but only when the property is nullable
items.explanation: required makes the deserializer reject a document without the member, so every older document breaks. The guide keeps required for members present since v1 and makes additions nullable or defaulted.

items.front: Two GC rules worth saying out loud in a review
items.back: 1) A collection costs time proportional to what survives, not to what died. 2) The worst object survives gen0 and then dies (the midlife crisis): you paid the copy for nothing. LOH: 85,000 bytes or more, collected only with gen2, not compacted by default.

items.front: When does a disposable type need a finalizer?
items.back: Only when it holds a raw unmanaged resource (IntPtr) directly. Own other disposables or a SafeHandle: IDisposable, no finalizer, seal it. Hold only memory: implement nothing. Inheritable raw IntPtr: full pattern with protected virtual Dispose(bool).

Exceptions for bugs (null/out-of-range arguments, use after dispose) and genuinely unexpected environment failures (database down, bad config at startup). Returns, Try or Result for expected outcomes (not found, validation, bad user input). Frequency breaks ties: per-item failures are not exceptional.

items.front: System.Text.Json contract versioning: read tolerantly, write strictly
items.back: Capture unknown members with [JsonExtensionData] and write them back; required only for v1 members; new members nullable or defaulted; pin wire names with [JsonPropertyName] before renaming.
